sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content: She is 75 years old. The day before admission, after drinking toddy in the afternoon, she suddenly became unable to move her right arm and leg and lost the ability to speak or respond to her daughters' commands — all around 6 p.m. She was taken to a local hospital, given inhalation therapy and cough syrup, and then referred on for further evaluation. She has no known history of diabetes, hypertension, prior stroke, asthma, or tuberculosis, but drinks toddy daily.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: unconscious, thin built; no icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or generalized edema
- Neurological exam: Glasgow Coma Scale E1V1M5; higher mental functions and cranial nerves could not be assessed; motor power markedly reduced on the right (1/5 in the arm, 2/5 in the leg) compared to the left (4/5 in both); right-sided limbs hypotonic, left-sided limbs hypertonic; reflexes reduced and asymmetric, with extensor plantar responses on both sides; sensory and cerebellar examination could not be assessed given her level of consciousness
- Cardiorespiratory and abdominal exam: unremarkable
- Investigations sent: imaging and blood work consistent with a stroke work-up (documented but not detailed in the available record)

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
She was started on intravenous ceftriaxone, a B-complex injection, and a proton pump inhibitor on the day of admission — an initial, largely supportive and infection-covering regimen appropriate for an unconscious patient with an unclear source of fever risk.

By day two, once her clinical picture was clearer, her treatment shifted toward secondary stroke prevention: aspirin and atorvastatin were added alongside her continued antibiotic and gastric protection, and this expanded regimen continued unchanged through day three. She was also shifted to an air bed to prevent pressure sores — a marker of her ongoing immobility and unconscious state as her stroke care continued.
